source_read: PDF, pp. 152-159 (all pages, including the reference list, checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi)

claims.overstatement: None material; the claim labels the source a position paper and attributes its statements to NAME. Precision points: the autopsy exception is delayed deaths after a (suspected) overdose, with review of the hospital record, rather than any death after a hospital stay; the 20-30% figure's references are, by title, clinical and medicolegal autopsy-discrepancy studies (1912-2003), none on drug deaths, plus one NCHS overdose count that measures no error (apparent mis-citation). The paper does cite one drug-death study (Dye et al., 2019) for external examination being less accurate even with strong scene findings, without a figure.
claims.note: Checked on rendered pages: autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected, one exception (p. 153); no published study showing external examination as accurate (p. 153); up to 20-30% (p. 153; refs on p. 158); insensitive indicator and eight circumstances for toxicology (p. 154).

anchors.extracted: Position paper of a National Association of Medical Examiners expert panel, convened with CDC support to update the 2014 recommendations by answering six questions; presented as evidence-based best practice, but no search, selection or grading method is described (expert consensus, not a systematic review). Abstract item 4: the toxicology panel should be comprehensive.

anchors.locator: 'Which deaths require assumption of jurisdiction and performance of an autopsy?' › 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Autopsy is the most accurate means of determining cause of death; NAME's Forensic Autopsy Performance Standards call for autopsy in any death where intoxication is suspected; published evidence offers no substitute; external examination alone is less accurate when drugs are present (ref. 14) even with scene findings strongly suggesting overdose (ref. 15, Dye et al., 2019, a drug-death study, no figure given); postmortem CT judged experimental (one study: triad 100% specific, 26% sensitive for opioid death).

anchors.locator: 'Which deaths require ... an autopsy?' › 2nd paragraph; References 6, 8-13 (p. 158)
anchors.extracted: Panel recommends autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected as a possible cause (one exception); peer-reviewed articles showing that external examination plus strong evidence of illicit drug use is as accurate as autopsy have not been published; decades of articles show diagnoses in error against autopsy in up to 20-30% of cases (refs 6, 8-13). By title these are clinical autopsy-discrepancy studies (Cabot 1912; Lundberg & Voigt 1979, sudden death; Sarode 1993) and medicolegal studies of certification without autopsy (Asnaes & Paaske 1980; Vanatta & Petty 1987; Nashelsky & Lawrence 2003); none is specific to drug deaths, and ref. 8 is an NCHS count of overdose deaths 1999-2017, not an accuracy study (apparent mis-citation).

NAME standards allow deferring autopsy in delayed deaths due to overdose or suspected overdose; the panel agrees, provided the medical record from hospital admission to death is reviewed and admission blood or urine is sought.

anchors.locator: 'When is it appropriate or necessary to perform toxicology testing?' › 1st paragraph and numbered list
anchors.extracted: History, investigative information and autopsy combined are an insensitive indicator of drug intoxication (refs 29, 30); quick urine screening kits give incomplete evidence, false positives and no confirmation, so are inadequate for establishing cause of death; panel recommends toxicology that identifies and quantifies controlled, illicit and relevant novel drugs in every decedent meeting any of eight circumstances (drug-use history; scene evidence of drug use; autopsy signs of drug use; massive lung oedema or froth without other explanation; suspected drug couriers; no unequivocal cause at autopsy; a natural cause where a drug may also play a role; traumatic deaths).

claims.overstatement: 'without a cited test of these rules' is accurate only for the 6-acetylmorphine rule, which is stated without a citation. The morphine-to-codeine rule cites three empirical studies (refs 44-46: ratios in impaired drivers, ratios in heroin-related deaths, heroin toxicity without 6-AM, the last co-authored by the lead author). Whether these validate the rule against an independent standard cannot be judged from the position paper. Suggest: 'treats 6-acetylmorphine as sufficient evidence of heroin, without a citation, and a morphine-to-codeine ratio above 1 as possible evidence, citing studies of such ratios whose accuracy it does not report'.
claims.note: The two rules are described correctly (p. 156). The same paper also recommends certifying heroin rather than its metabolites and avoiding 'mixed drug intoxication' without named drugs (p. 156-157), the practices the claim says hide heroin; and it says lethal and sublethal concentrations cannot simply be told apart (p. 156), relevant also to cl_gen_deaths_level_cause, which does not cite this source.

anchors.locator: 'How does the interpretation of postmortem drug concentrations affect the certification ...?' › 6th paragraph; References 44-46 (p. 159)
anchors.extracted: 6-acetylmorphine in a sample is stated to be sufficient evidence to ascribe intoxication to heroin, with no citation (reasoning from heroin's rapid metabolism to 6-AM). Without 6-AM, heroin use can be inferred otherwise: morphine may come from morphine or codeine, but heroin carries codeine as a contaminant, so a blood morphine/codeine ratio above 1 may be considered evidence of heroin use (refs 44, 45), particularly with illicit drug paraphernalia (ref. 46); heroin in syringe residue is stronger evidence. The ratio rule cites three empirical studies: Ceder & Jones 2001 (ratios in blood of impaired drivers as evidence of heroin use), Jones & Holmgren 2011 (ratios in femoral blood in heroin-related poisoning deaths), Ellis et al. 2016 (heroin toxicity without detected 6-AM; co-authored by the lead author). Their accuracy against an independent standard is not reported here.
Recommended practice: list the generic names of all drugs that caused or contributed to death, and avoid vague terms such as mixed drug intoxication or polypharmacy without naming the drugs.

CDC instructs certifiers to list the parent drug, not metabolites; in the panel's worked example with 6-AM, morphine and codeine detected, certify heroin rather than 6-acetylmorphine, morphine and codeine.

Telling drugs that played a role from drugs merely present is complex; concentrations help, but there is no simple way to tell lethal from sublethal concentrations in an individual because of postmortem redistribution and tolerance.

key_findings.correction: Quotation checked: exact, 7 words. The card does not record the citations behind the ratio rule; see 'missed'.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, high (no search, no appraisal).

The autopsy recommendation therefore does not rest only on general autopsy-discrepancy studies (replication.where_it_stands).
